- self_reference: The object contains a sentence describing itself, and the description checks out verbatim as true — it points back to itself in one step, with no climb through levels and no reference to a second system.
- recursion: The whole is generated from smaller copies of itself by the same rule; however many levels you enter, that many you exit, terminating at a base case and then returning level by level along the original path.
- nesting: Each time a new level is entered, the previous level is never returned to; depth only ever increases.
- cycle: Following same-level causal arrows through n>=3 mutually distinct events returns you to the starting event; one lap restores everything verbatim (no escalation, no growth, no flip), all points equal in status, no hierarchy.
- symmetry: The sequence of events read backwards is item-for-item identical to reading it forwards; folded at the temporal midpoint, it coincides point by point.
- alternation: Exactly two states strictly take turns: adjacent items always differ, items one apart are always the same, the period is constantly two, without a single exception.
- spiral: Each time it comes back around to the same bearing it grows one notch by the same fixed ratio, never returning to the original scale.
- convergence: Multiple threads, mutually unaware, each advance on their own and finally all merge into the same endpoint, and there it ends.
- bottleneck: Each of the two shores is internally multiply connected, but every path between the shores must pass through one and the same midway point, continuing separately beyond it; deleting that point splits the graph into exactly two still-connected halves, rather than shattering it into isolated pieces.
- symmetry_breaking: One rule covers the whole field, with exactly one precisely locatable violation; the violation is unique and everywhere else is without exception.
- strange_loop: Climbing step by step up the hierarchy of 'who narrates whom', the final step nevertheless lands back at the starting point; no consistent level can be assigned.
- figure_ground: Figure and ground complementarily fill the whole canvas and the ground itself forms a figure: the second half takes the first half's ground as its figure and the first half's figure as its ground, while the narrated events and their order remain unchanged (not reversed order, and not a translation between two vocabularies).
- isomorphism: Between two things made of entirely different material there exists a one-to-one dictionary preserving all operations and relations, translatable term by term in the same order, without a single exception.
- mobius: Traveling once around the band returns you to the starting place with orientation flipped (left and right exchanged); only after two laps is everything restored point by point.
- braiding: Three or more strands cross adjacently several times; the final arrangement of the ends equals exactly the composition of all the crossings in order, and the order cannot be freely exchanged.
- interference: Two patterns with different periods, each monotonously repeating on its own, are superposed and a new period larger than either original emerges.
- tiling: Shift the entire pattern by one cell and it coincides exactly with the original, seamless and without overlap, without a single exception.
- hub: Between any two endpoints stands only the center point; remove the center and the whole graph shatters into isolated points.
- diagonalization: A table enumerated row by row; the new row built by flipping each entry along the diagonal is guaranteed to differ from row n at position n, hence differs from every row — forever outside the table. Unlike self_reference (an object pointing back to itself in one step): the diagonal element does not talk about itself; the attack targets the table's entire enumeration, not itself. Crucially unlike symmetry_breaking (exactly one isolated violation in an otherwise regular field): here it is not one anomalous cell but n systematic differences along a moving diagonal — row n differs at position n, the position shifting right by one each row, exactly one per row, and this construction guarantees 'not equal to any row'; symmetry_breaking is a single-point flaw that neither escapes nor refutes any enumeration.
- infinite_descent: Every case forces a strictly smaller case of the same kind, and the natural numbers admit no bottomless descending chain, so the first case does not exist at all — the proof's blade swings backwards: not advancing to an end, but cancelling the beginning. Exactly opposite to recursion: recursion exits as many levels as it enters and stands on the existence of a base case; descent stands on the absence of one and condemns every witness to nonexistence. Unlike zeno_halving: Zeno's steps shrink by a fixed ratio, total length finite, the journey completes; descent's decrease is arbitrary but each step is an integer, the chain is forbidden by well-ordering, the conclusion is 'impossible'. Unlike contraction_fixed_point: contraction iterates forever and converges to a genuinely existing fixed point; the descending chain converges to nothing, must hit floor 1 in finitely many steps, so the whole chain together with its starting point is judged nonexistent. Opposite in direction to ordinal_ascent: ordinal ascent is unbounded upward with every level real; descent is bounded below with the whole chain illusory. Unlike invariant_barrier: no conserved quantity is invoked; the only killing move is that strict decrease cannot go on forever.
- coprime_orbit: On a ring of n points, jump with a fixed stride k, connecting as you go: if the stride is coprime to the ring length, a single stroke visits every point before closing; if not, the ring splits into gcd parts. Unlike cycle (adjacent arrows closing head-to-tail in one lap): the large stride weaves a star shape, traversal is conditional on coprimality, and there is a failure mode — not coprime means splitting. Unlike interference (two independent periods superposed, an lcm-sized larger period emerging): here there is only one orbit and one number-theoretic condition. Unlike hub (relaying through a center): there is no central point at all; traversal is guaranteed purely by gcd(k,n)=1.
- pigeonhole: More items than cages forces two into the same cage: the collision is proved certain, yet no one can point to where it happens. Unlike convergence (all threads, knowingly or not, ending at the same KNOWN point): here counting only guarantees that at some UNSPECIFIED place at least two meet; no witness is constructed. Unlike bottleneck (every path forced through the same midway point): there is no forced path and no relay hub, only a single count.
- projective_duality: Within a single system, two classes of roles are swapped wholesale and every relational proposition remains true; swapping twice restores the original verbatim (an involution, sigma^2=id). Exclusions: unlike isomorphism (a relation-preserving dictionary between two heterogeneous materials) — duality is a role swap inside one and the same material and is necessarily an involution; unlike figure_ground (figure and ground complementarily filling one canvas) — duality produces two pictures each complete in itself, not relying on negative space; unlike transformed_canon (the same theme reappearing in a lagged voice under a fixed transformation) — duality is a wholesale sequential restatement that swaps role vocabulary while truth values stay unchanged, not a voice-level pitch/time transformation; unlike chirality (mirror image and original cannot be superposed, the point being 'it does not fit') — the two dual statements both hold within the same system and the swap restores everything exactly; unlike mobius (the flip requires traveling one full lap along a path) — duality has no path, it is an immediate wholesale role swap; unlike symmetry (item-by-item reversed palindrome) — duality does not reverse order, it only swaps roles.
- contraction_fixed_point: One and the same rule is applied again and again to its own output; each step shrinks the distance to the endpoint by a fixed ratio q<1, finally resting at the one point that the rule sends back to itself unchanged — the endpoint is not announced in advance but selected from inside the rule by the fixed-point property f(x*)=x*. Unlike spiral (fixed-ratio growth, never returning to the original scale): the direction is reversed and there is a real endpoint; unlike convergence (many mutually unaware threads ending at one place): here there is from start to finish a single self-iterating chain; unlike recursion (as many exits as entries, returning level by level to the caller): the iteration only collapses forward and never returns; unlike zeno_halving (infinitely shrinking segments laid end to end, the point being that the infinite sum is exactly a finite whole): here the point is that the endpoint is fixed by the map — what is checked is f(x*)=x*, not a sum of distances; unlike negative_feedback (alternating over- and under-shoot around a target announced at the outset): the target must not be pre-announced, no sign alternation is required, one-sided collapse suffices, and the endpoint certifies itself by its own fixedness.
- aperiodic_tiling: Everywhere obeying the same local matching rules, seamlessly covering the whole plane, yet no translation whatsoever makes the whole picture coincide with itself; at the same time any local patch reappears within a bounded gap everywhere — 'seen before, never repeated'. Exclusion clauses: unlike tiling (shift one cell and the whole coincides; here it is provable that no translational period exists at all); unlike symmetry_breaking (a periodic background with exactly one locatable violation; here there is no violation anywhere, yet no period exists at all); unlike spiral (phi here is the frequency ratio of the two tile kinds, not level-by-level fixed-ratio growth; the figure has no self-similar scaling center); unlike transformed_canon (the same theme reappearing verbatim under a fixed transformation; here no block ever recurs exactly at a fixed interval); unlike interference (two periods superposed still yield an lcm period; here the limiting structure's frequency is irrational, so there is never a period).

options.A: Cutting a □ strip along its center line yields a single connected strip: an orientable, two-sided strip twice as long, not two strips; in the standard embedding in R^3 it has four half-twists (720°). Equivalently, intrinsically, the complement of the center line in the strip is connected.
options.B: If f has positive integer period p and g has positive integer period q, then lcm(p,q) is a period of f+g (not necessarily the least). When gcd(p,q) = 1, the phase pair (n mod p, n mod q) runs through all pq combinations exactly once every pq steps as n advances, returning to (0,0) (by the Chinese remainder theorem); hence the two patterns are □ only once every pq steps.

options.D: Hairy Ball Theorem (a corollary of Poincaré–Hopf): On every even-dimensional sphere S^{2n} (χ = 2 ≠ 0), every continuous tangent vector field has a zero; moreover, on S² one can construct a tangent vector field with exactly one zero (pull back a constant vector field on the plane by stereographic projection; the unique zero is at the north pole and has index 2). Mara lived above a cobbler shop where the street smelled of rain, leather, and plum cakes. Her father sewed soles by the window, and Mara swept curls of brown hide into a basket for garden beds.

Round and round again, one person.

The person was Old Tovin, who came in with a split boot and no coin till barley time. Mara stitched it while her father nodded, and she tucked a warm bun in the toe.

Round and round again, one family mended boots, shared soup, and smiled.

That family was the Brindleys, seven in a cottage with blue shutters. When Tovin told them of the bun, they brought Mara a pot of bean soup and patched her father's torn apron with red thread.

Round and round again, one village brought wool, apples, nails, songs, and steady hands, until Mara's small kindness had warmed every doorstep by dusk.

So the miller fixed the shop latch, the baker left seed cakes, the shepherd combed soft wool for winter socks, and children lined their shoes neatly by Mara's bench. Her father laughed for the first time since snowmelt.

Round and round again, one kingdom heard how a cobbler's daughter saved a lamb, lent a shawl, lifted a cart, and taught glad neighbors to pass on help, so bells rang from hill farms to sea towns, and every child kept a crumb for the next hungry bird.

Years later, Mara's sign showed a boot with a bun peeping out. Travelers stopped to ask why, and she only smiled, stitched their soles tight, and sent them away walking kinder than they came.

Round and round again one person.

That person was Mara, and she watered the little twig from a blue cup each morning. When frost silvered the grass, she wrapped the stem in wool from an old mitten and sang to it before school.

Round and round again, one family carried baskets under apple trees together.

By midsummer the young tree gave six small apples, sharp and bright. Mara's mother baked them with oats, her father mended the fence, and her brothers set bowls on the sill for anyone passing hungry.

Round and round again, one village brought ladders, songs, aprons, and sleepy children to Mara's orchard at dawn, sharing sweet windfalls with travelers gladly.

An old peddler said he had never tasted kinder fruit. He traded three copper pans for a jar of Mara's jam, then told the next inn, and the next mill, and the next far farm.

Round and round again, one kingdom tasted Mara's golden jam at winter feasts, and the smallest spoonful carried news of the hill, the bees, the red gate, and the child who planted a single pip beside her grandmother's well, so all hungry hands could share together in peace.

When Mara grew grey, she gave each visiting child a pip wrapped in brown paper. She told them, Plant it where someone lonely may find shade, and leave a bowl ready on the sill.

options.A: Tilda the tailor lived at the edge of Briar Hollow, where geese slept under wagons. Her workshop smelled of wool, beeswax, and the apple tea she kept warm for visitors. Every winter she sewed coats for children who had outgrown last year's sleeves. Few coins came her way, but no child left cold. In the same village lived Bram, a shepherd boy with more kindness than buttons. Rain had spoiled his only cloak, and frost was silvering the fields. So Bram brought Tilda a basket of chestnuts and asked for any scrap she could spare. Tilda smiled and set him by the stove with a mug of tea. Little patches lay in heaps, blue as dusk and green as moss. Each scrap had come from a neighbor's coat, cap, apron, or blanket. The oldest craftsperson in the village had taught Tilda to save such pieces. Thread by thread, she joined them while Bram shelled chestnuts and sang softly. Evening settled, and the geese tucked their beaks beneath their wings. Rag by rag, she hid the title sentence along the lining in tiny red stitches. Soon the cloak looked humble outside, yet merry within. On the collar she placed a brass button shaped like a star. From the stove, Bram watched the cloth seem to gather every hearth in Briar Hollow. Tilda tied the last knot before moonrise. He put the cloak on, and it fitted as though the wind had measured him kindly. In its warmth, Bram felt the baker's oven, the miller's mittens, and Tilda's apple tea. Snow began that night, soft at first, then thick as feathers. Still Bram drove the sheep toward the byre, holding his lantern low. The smallest lamb slipped through a gap and vanished into white grass. Over the hill Bram followed, though the drifts nipped at his knees. Red stitches inside the cloak glimmered whenever his lantern swung near. Yet Bram had no time to read them, for the lamb bleated from a ditch. Stooping, he lifted the creature and tucked it against his chest. Slowly he turned homeward, but the snow had covered every cart track. Each gust blew out the lantern and stole his breath. Near the old thorn tree, the brass star button caught a shred of moon. Then the red stitches shone bright enough to guide his fingers along the lining. Every word warmed under his touch like bread from an oven. Not knowing why, Bram spoke the sewn sentence aloud to the snow. Cold eased from his hands, and the cloak brightened as if remembering its making. Even the lamb stopped shivering and pressed its nose to the cloth. Somewhere beyond the white field, the village bell answered once. Step by step, Bram followed the bell until roofs rose from the storm. People ran out with blankets, broth, and joyful scolding. Edda the baker kissed the lamb on its woolly head. Laughter filled Tilda's shop when Bram told how the red words had glowed. Later, Tilda only winked and mended the torn hem. The cloak passed from Bram to his sister, then to a niece, then to a grandson. Hearths changed, wagons broke, and new geese slept under them. In every cold season, someone found the red stitches and smiled. Some wore the cloak to fetch wood, some to carry babies, some to visit lonely neighbors. Travelers said Briar Hollow had the warmest old cloak in three valleys. In time, no one knew who first paid for it with chestnuts. The cloak knew enough, and kept its red words safe. Long after Tilda's kettle was gone, the sentence still sat inside the cloth. Every reader who found it saw that it told just what it was.

options.C: There was a child named Mina in the pear orchard. Her grandmother kept a narrow path between the trees. Every dawn, Mina carried a tin pail for the fallen fruit. From the gate, the lane smelled of rain and honey. In a low branch, she found a small cedar box. Rain had darkened the lid, but the latch was bright. Some blue thread was knotted around its handle. Two ants marched over the painted side. Long ago, the box had belonged to Aunt Nella. Inside, there was a note folded twice. The box carried a sentence that read I am the little box that keeps Aunt Nella's seeds. That was true, for the seeds rattled gently within. Each word fit the wood like a key in a pocket. Rainclouds slid away, and Mina laughed. Soon, the craftsperson who made the box came by with plums. On his sleeve, he wore dust from the workshop. For he had carved the lid with a goose and a pear tree. That autumn, he had given the box to Aunt Nella. Her hands had planted sweet beans and marigolds in it. In a scarf fold, she hid the title sentence until she reached the door. She had meant to return the box before supper. So she tucked it under her arm and walked home. The road dipped past the brook and the white cow. Old Mrs Pike waved from her gate. Roses climbed her fence in red tangles. Yonder, the bell in the chapel sang thin and clear. Sunlight found the box and warmed the cedar. Soon, Mina felt as if the little note were singing. Even the hens in the yard paused to listen. Near the door, Aunt Nella peered over her spectacles. Tenderly, she opened the box and smiled. Every bean inside belonged to spring. No one in the village forgot that day. Children came to hear the tale by the hearth. Each asked why the note could speak so plainly. She told them that honest words are light on the tongue. Snow came later, with hard edges on the pond. Pine smoke curled from the chimneys at dusk. Elder Tom brought cider in a jug. Little Mina kept the empty box on her shelf. Later, she wrote her own name under the lid. Then she laughed because it fit so neatly. Her grandmother said a true thing can wear a small coat. In the moonrise, the orchard looked like a silver bowl. Stars shone through the bare branches. That winter, the room smelled of beeswax and pine. Inside, she planed a board for spring. The board would hold new notes for new gifts. Larks would sing before the frost left the grass. Even now, Mina remembers the box and its plain true words.

options.B: Tall cedars shaded the potter's yard at Brindle Hill. Hannah kept the kiln there with her son Milo and a gray cat named Peat. Every morning, villagers brought cracked bowls, dull jugs, and wishes for wedding plates. For each hand she found a fair shape in the clay. In winter, the yard smelled of wet earth and apple smoke. Rainy days sent children under the shed roof to watch the wheel hum. Sometimes Hannah let them press thumbprints into scraps. The smallest thumbprint always belonged to Orra, the shepherd's niece. Last frost, Orra carried in a cup broken clean in two. Even its handle seemed ashamed, hanging by a thread of glaze. The cup had been her mother's, and she feared the sheep bells would sound lonely without it. Tenderly, Hannah set both halves on a cloth. Everyone grew quiet while she mixed slip as pale as cream. Rosy slip gleamed on Hannah's fingers as she worked. Softly, Milo fed chips of pine to the kiln. Outside, the cat guarded the doorway from sparrows. From a shelf, Hannah chose a narrow iron point. Then she mended the cup so neatly that Orra forgot to sniffle. Hannah promised a small gift besides, if Orra could wait until moonrise. In the workshop, she shaped a lid no larger than a plum. She brushed it blue, the color of dusk after rain. Soon the kiln glowed like a loaf with fire in its crust. Through the long afternoon, neighbors came and went with gossip and warm bread. Orra stayed, drowsy but hopeful, counting swallows in the eaves. Red light filled the yard when Hannah drew out the little cup. Yet the gift was not finished, for the lid still held a secret. She cooled it in a basin and rubbed away a bead of ash. Small signs ran around its rim, tidy as seeds in a row. Even Milo bent close, though he had helped with the firing. No one could read them at first, not even the schoolmaster passing by. Then Hannah turned the lid slowly in Orra's hands. Each sign gave the next word of a plain saying. Now Orra read aloud, and her cheeks shone. Come home whole, little cup, and keep the lamb girl merry. Everyone laughed, for that was just what the cup had done. Still, Hannah winked and tapped the rim. Some village craftsperson may be shy, she said, but a shy craft may speak truly. Peat sneezed at the smoke, which made the children cheer. Every bowl on the shelf seemed to sit taller. Later, Orra carried the cup across the pasture with both hands. Lambs gathered near her knees, nosing the blue lid. That night, she poured milk into the mended cup and shared it with Milo. Hannah watched from the door, pleased as a hearth in snow. In the rim she hid the title sentence, though Orra only knew it as a blessing. So the cup kept telling exactly what it was. The village trusted Hannah more after that, not because she boasted. Instead, each pot left her yard with honest clay, honest fire, and a word that fit. To this day, when a child breaks a treasure, the family brings the pieces up Brindle Hill. Little Peat's grandkitten sits by the path and blinks at sparrows. Every repaired cup goes home with its own true saying.

options.A: Tilda the tailor lived at the edge of Briar Hollow, where geese slept under wagons. Her workshop smelled of wool, beeswax, and the apple tea she kept warm for visitors. Every winter she sewed coats for children who had outgrown last year's sleeves. Few coins came her way, but no child left cold. In the same village lived Bram, a shepherd boy with more kindness than buttons. Rain had spoiled his only cloak, and frost was silvering the fields. So Bram brought Tilda a basket of chestnuts and asked for any scrap she could spare. Tilda smiled and set him by the stove with a mug of tea. Little patches lay in heaps, blue as dusk and green as moss. Each scrap had come from a neighbor's coat, cap, apron, or blanket. The oldest craftsperson in the village had taught Tilda to save such pieces. Thread by thread, she joined them while Bram shelled chestnuts and sang softly. Evening settled, and the geese tucked their beaks beneath their wings. Rag by rag, she hid the title sentence along the lining in tiny red stitches. Soon the cloak looked humble outside, yet merry within. On the collar she placed a brass button shaped like a star. From the stove, Bram watched the cloth seem to gather every hearth in Briar Hollow. Tilda tied the last knot before moonrise. He put the cloak on, and it fitted as though the wind had measured him kindly. In its warmth, Bram felt the baker's oven, the miller's mittens, and Tilda's apple tea. Snow began that night, soft at first, then thick as feathers. Still Bram drove the sheep toward the byre, holding his lantern low. The smallest lamb slipped through a gap and vanished into white grass. Over the hill Bram followed, though the drifts nipped at his knees. Red stitches inside the cloak glimmered whenever his lantern swung near. Yet Bram had no time to read them, for the lamb bleated from a ditch. Stooping, he lifted the creature and tucked it against his chest. Slowly he turned homeward, but the snow had covered every cart track. Each gust blew out the lantern and stole his breath. Near the old thorn tree, the brass star button caught a shred of moon. Then the red stitches shone bright enough to guide his fingers along the lining. Every word warmed under his touch like bread from an oven. Not knowing why, Bram spoke the sewn sentence aloud to the snow. Cold eased from his hands, and the cloak brightened as if remembering its making. Even the lamb stopped shivering and pressed its nose to the cloth. Somewhere beyond the white field, the village bell answered once. Step by step, Bram followed the bell until roofs rose from the storm. People ran out with blankets, broth, and joyful scolding. Edda the baker kissed the lamb on its woolly head. Laughter filled Tilda's shop when Bram told how the red words had glowed. Later, Tilda only winked and mended the torn hem. The cloak passed from Bram to his sister, then to a niece, then to a grandson. Hearths changed, wagons broke, and new geese slept under them. In every cold season, someone found the red stitches and smiled. Some wore the cloak to fetch wood, some to carry babies, some to visit lonely neighbors. Travelers said Briar Hollow had the warmest old cloak in three valleys. In time, no one knew who first paid for it with chestnuts. The cloak knew enough, and kept its red words safe. Long after Tilda's kettle was gone, the sentence still sat inside the cloth. Every reader who found it saw that it told just what it was.

items.text: Fedorov's theorem (1891): There are exactly 17 plane crystallographic groups, counted up to □. Moreover, there are exactly three edge-to-edge □ of the plane by a single regular polygon: equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons, because the interior angle at each vertex must divide 360°, and the interior angle of a regular n-gon, (n-2)·180°/n, divides 360° only when n = 3, 4, 6.

options.B: If f has positive integer period p and g has positive integer period q, then lcm(p,q) is a period of f+g (not necessarily the least). When gcd(p,q) = 1, the phase pair (n mod p, n mod q) runs through all pq combinations exactly once every pq steps as n advances, returning to (0,0) (by the Chinese remainder theorem); hence the two patterns are □ only once every pq steps.

Consequently, □ of even length admit a proper 2-coloring with the colors □ around the □, whereas □ of odd length do not; moreover, every connected bipartite graph (in particular, a path P_n) has a proper 2-coloring that is unique up to interchanging the two colors.

options.C: At the hill orchard, old Mara kept two baskets of stones, broad yellow ones and slim blue ones. "Pick kindly, Tom." Tom set a yellow stone by the gate, and its nick kissed the notch of a blue stone. All morning the children added stones wherever the little marks agreed, leaving no bare earth between roots. "This one remembers me." By noon, every path seemed familiar, yet no path lay just where Tom expected it. "Seen before, never same." Mara laughed softly and showed him how a broad stone often found more broad cousins than slim ones. Still, the slim stones were never lonely, for each held a corner that called another child closer. "No place is the master." They walked from pear trees to bee hives, and every small handful of stones came again soon. But the whole orchard refused to slide into its earlier self, however far Tom dragged his gaze. "Then it is alive." A blackbird hopped over the joins, finding every edge snug, every crossing tidy, every crumb of soil covered. "Nothing is lost here." When evening cooled the ladders, Mara counted their baskets and smiled at the yellow stones left fewer. Tom counted the laid stones instead, and found yellow ahead of blue by a pleasing handful. "Tomorrow, bring the neighbors." So next day more hands came, and each new child could begin anywhere without mending a mistake. "Where does it end?" Mara pointed past the last apple tree, where grass waited, and Tom carried two stones onward.

No one could slide the whole floor a single step and make it match itself, not the dockmaster, not the miller, not even Mara with her strong hands. "See," she said. Still, if a baby dropped a crumb or a sailor lost a button, some kind hand would find an old likeness nearby before long, as if the lane kept good memory for small things. That was why the folk came from far off to sweep the stones with their eyes, and they went home lighter, as though they had heard a cradle song from the ground. "Good night," said the miller. At dawn, the first gulls found no end to the kindness of the lane, only more quiet places where a step could rest and go on. "Come back," sang Mara. items.text: Cantor's □ closed interval theorem: If a sequence of bounded closed intervals satisfies [a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] ⊆ [a_n, b_n] for every n, then ⋂_{n≥1}[a_n, b_n] is nonempty; if, in addition, b_n − a_n → 0, then the intersection is exactly the singleton {ξ}, where ξ = sup_n a_n = inf_n b_n.

options.A: Fermat (his account of the method appears in a 1659 letter to Carcavi; the full proof survives in marginal note 45 to his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica, published by his son Samuel in 1670): a right triangle with integer side lengths cannot have square area — proved by infinite □; consequently, x^4+y^4=z^2 has no positive integer solutions, and therefore x^4+y^4=z^4 has no positive integer solutions (the n=4 case of Fermat's Last Theorem).
options.B: Newman’s lemma (1942): a terminating (strongly normalizing) abstract rewriting system that is locally □ is globally □; hence, for every element, all of its reduction sequences end in the same unique normal form. Banach □ theorem (1922): every □ self-map of a complete metric space has a unique □, and the iterates from any initial value □ to that same □.
options.C: Dyck words of length 2n, full binary trees with exactly n internal nodes, and triangulations of a convex (n+2)-gon are three families of objects all counted by the Catalan number C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1) (Euler–Segner enumeration; see Stanley, Catalan Numbers), and there are explicit bijections between each pair.
options.D: Banach □ theorem (S. Banach 1922, Fundamenta Mathematicae 3, 133–181): a □ mapping on a complete metric space has a unique □, Picard iteration from any initial value converges to it, and the a priori error satisfies d(x_n,x*) ≤ q^n/(1−q)·d(x_1,x_0).
